studies.authors: Knaggs RD, Crighton IM, Cobby TF, Fletcher AJP, Hobbs GJ
studies.title: The pupillary effects of intravenous morphine, codeine, and tramadol in volunteers
studies.design: volunteer study; IV morphine, codeine, tramadol or saline placebo with pupil diameter measured every 30 min over 6 h, analysed by repeated-measures ANOVA (randomisation and blinding not stated in the available record)
studies.population: healthy volunteers
studies.condition: IV morphine 0.125 mg/kg; codeine 1 mg/kg; tramadol 1.25 mg/kg; placebo 10 mL 0.9% saline
studies.device: pupil densitometer (model not stated)

measures.units: % change from baseline
measures.evidence_text: Morphine and codeine produced a 26% decrease in pupil diameter (P < 0.001), which gradually returned to baseline over the study period.

measures.units: mm (no value reported)
measures.evidence_text: Tramadol: no significant change until 150 minutes, then a significant reduction in pupil diameter for the rest of the study period (P < 0.01). Delayed onset; no magnitude given.

measures.units: mm (no value reported)
measures.evidence_text: "No significant change in pupil diameter was observed after placebo."

studies.authors: Bokoch MP, Behrends M, Neice A, Larson MD
studies.title: Fentanyl, an agonist at the mu opioid receptor, depresses pupillary unrest
studies.design: experimental volunteer study plus observational preoperative patient cohort
studies.population: 8 volunteers and 20 patients scheduled for knee arthroscopy who received fentanyl as premedication
studies.condition: fentanyl 1 mcg/kg IV (described as a moderate dose)
studies.device: infrared pupillometer; 16-s recordings sampled at about 33 Hz, pupillary unrest quantified by fast Fourier transform with blink-artifact and baseline-drift filtering

measures.units: % depression of pupillary unrest (spectral power, ambient light)
measures.p_or_stat: 40 +/- 20% (mean +/- SD of the percent depression)
measures.evidence_text: A moderate fentanyl dose of 1 mcg/kg depressed pupillary unrest by 40 +/- 20%; recovery from the drug effect was observed. Light excitation of the Edinger-Westphal nucleus augmented pupillary unrest.

studies.authors: Richman JE, McAndrew KG, Decker D, Mullaney SC
studies.title: An evaluation of pupil size standards used by police officers for detecting drug impairment
studies.volume_pages: 75(3) (page range not confirmed from the author-version PDF available, which prints '75:xxx-xx'; commonly cited as 175-182)
studies.design: cross-sectional normative observational study with videographic validation in a 20% random subsample
studies.population: 250 drug-free adult volunteers (500 eyes), mean age 29.2 (+/-6.1) years; 87% men, 13% women; 90% white; 40% blue/hazel/green and 60% brown irides; 82% with a negative urine drug screen within the preceding 30 days
studies.condition: no drug administered - normative reference distribution against which the DRE/DEC pupil-size standard is judged
studies.device: pupil measurement under three standardised lighting conditions, validated against videography in 50 subjects (instrument model not stated in the available text)

measures.units: mm (room light)
measures.p_or_stat: repeated-measures ANOVA across the three lighting conditions F = 3.45; p < 0.0001
measures.evidence_text: Room light: mean (SD) 3.86 (0.93) mm, median 3.62 mm, in 250 drug-free volunteers. No drug was administered, so there is no impaired condition.

measures.units: mm (near-total darkness)
measures.p_or_stat: repeated-measures ANOVA across the three lighting conditions F = 3.45; p < 0.0001
measures.evidence_text: Near-total darkness: mean (SD) 6.41 (1.55) mm, median 6.45 mm, in 250 drug-free volunteers.

measures.units: mm (direct light)
measures.p_or_stat: repeated-measures ANOVA across the three lighting conditions F = 3.45; p < 0.0001
measures.evidence_text: Direct light: mean (SD) 3.35 (0.72) mm, median 3.40 mm, in 250 drug-free volunteers.

measures.units: mm (lower and upper bound of the DEC 'normal non-impaired' pupil range applied under all three lighting conditions)
measures.p_or_stat: iris colour had no significant effect (F = 0.16, NS); blue group (n=100) 3.86 / 6.39 / 3.34 mm vs brown group (n=150) 3.89 / 6.55 / 3.34 mm for room light / darkness / direct light
measures.evidence_text: The Drug Evaluation and Classification standard treats 3.0 to 6.5 mm as the normal non-impaired pupil range under all three conditions. The authors conclude the range 'might be too sensitive' (abstract) / 'may be too narrow' (discussion), and that impairment decisions rest on the totality of the evidence rather than pupil size alone. The percentage of subjects falling outside 3.0-6.5 mm is not reported.

studies.authors: Sørensen VOI, Uhrenholt S, Stokholm J, Christensen T, Bestle MH
studies.title: The Influence of Opioids on Pupil Initial Diameter and Pupillary Dilation Velocity in ICU Patients
studies.design: prospective observational sub-study; daily paired blood sampling and pupillary light reflex measurement, analysed with linear mixed models
studies.population: acutely admitted, mixed-diagnosis intensive care unit patients
studies.condition: clinically administered opioids with blood concentrations quantified by mass spectrometry; the association was driven mainly by fentanyl

measures.units: mm/s increase in pupillary dilation velocity per 1 mm increase in pre-stimulus pupil diameter
measures.evidence_text: Pupil size before a light stimulus was closely associated with dilation velocity after the stimulus: velocity increased by 0.2 mm/s for each 1 mm increase in pre-stimulus pupil diameter (95% CI 0.2-0.3, p < 0.001). This is a confound to note: dilation velocity is largely a function of starting diameter.

measures.units: mm/s (no value reported)
measures.p_or_stat: stated as concentration-dependent; no coefficient given in the available abstract
measures.evidence_text: "In this mixed ICU population, fentanyl in blood was associated with slower pupillary dilation velocity, in a concentration-dependent manner." The editorial comment notes several co-administered drug classes affecting autonomic function may have been present.

measures.units: mm (no value reported)
measures.evidence_text: "Fentanyl was associated with smaller pupil size and slower dilation velocity." No means or SDs are given in the available abstract.

studies.authors: Kongsgaard UE, Høiseth G
studies.title: Dynamic assessment of the pupillary reflex in patients on high-dose opioids
studies.volume_pages: 19(3):465- (start page 465 per the publisher's article listing; end page not confirmed)
studies.design: observational case-control study comparing chronic high-dose opioid cancer patients (split into dose-increase and stable-dose subgroups) with opioid-free healthy volunteers; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02247024
studies.population: 63 cancer pain patients (25 men, 38 women; median age 61 y, IQR 53-69, range 22-86) on opioids for at least 4 weeks at a minimum of 60 mg/day oral morphine equivalents, and 20 opioid-free volunteers (9 men, 11 women; median age 55 y, IQR 34-61, range 23-68)
studies.condition: chronic oral/transdermal opioids, median 250 mg/day oral morphine equivalents (IQR 150-370, range 50-840), median 2 months on opioids; oxycodone (45 patients), morphine (21), transdermal fentanyl (12), methadone (9), many on more than one. Median blood concentrations (micromol/L): morphine 0.128, M3G 1.246, M6G 0.310, oxycodone 0.261, fentanyl 0.004, methadone 0.366
studies.device: AlgiScan (Idmed, Marseille, France) portable monocular infrared video pupillometer, with a silicone eyecup blocking external light from the test eye

measures.units: mm (baseline = 20 opioid-free volunteers; impaired = 36 patients whose opioid dose was increased in the last 14 days)
measures.p_or_stat: one-way ANOVA F(2,75) = 32.53, p = 0.000; Tukey increase-vs-no-increase p = 0.008, no-increase-vs-volunteers p = 0.000; age-adjusted ANCOVA increase-vs-volunteers p = 0.006, no-increase-vs-volunteers F(1,39) = 3.32, p = 0.076
measures.evidence_text: Table 3 baseline pupil diameter: dose-increase group 3.71 +/- 0.79 mm, stable-dose group 4.73 +/- 0.79 mm, healthy volunteers 5.51 +/- 0.89 mm. The authors conclude 'tolerance to miosis takes place in some patients who are on a stable opioid dose' - age-adjusted, the stable-dose group did not differ significantly from volunteers while the dose-increase group did.

measures.units: % constriction ('variation'); baseline = opioid-free volunteers, impaired = dose-increase patients
measures.p_or_stat: one-way ANOVA F(2,75) = 8.1, p = 0.001
measures.evidence_text: Table 3 constriction amplitude ('variation'): dose-increase 30.9 +/- 7.0%, stable-dose 35.9 +/- 8.0%, volunteers 40.2 +/- 10.8%.

measures.units: mm/s; baseline = opioid-free volunteers, impaired = dose-increase patients
measures.evidence_text: Table 3 constriction velocity: dose-increase 3.01 +/- 0.82 mm/s, stable-dose 3.89 +/- 0.94 mm/s, volunteers 5.12 +/- 1.09 mm/s.

measures.units: ms; baseline = opioid-free volunteers, impaired = dose-increase patients
measures.p_or_stat: one-way ANOVA F(2,74) = 0.44, p = 0.64 (not significant)
measures.evidence_text: Table 3 latency to constriction: dose-increase 276 +/- 242 ms, stable-dose 243 +/- 44 ms, volunteers 237 +/- 32 ms; the three groups did not differ (p = 0.64). Latency was the one pupillary parameter unaffected by chronic opioid exposure.

measures.units: Pearson r between age and baseline pupil size in opioid-free volunteers
measures.evidence_text: Age and baseline pupil size in volunteers: r = -0.776, n = 20, p = 0.000. Directly relevant to the age-related miosis confound. Correlations of pupillary measures with total oral morphine equivalents were weak and non-significant (baseline r = -0.237, p = 0.070; variation r = -0.247, p = 0.057; velocity r = -0.220, p = 0.098; latency r = 0.100, p = 0.453), and blood opioid/metabolite concentrations showed no significant correlation with any pupillary measure.

studies.authors: Rollins MD, Feiner JR, Lee JM, Shah S, Larson M
studies.title: Pupillary Effects of High-dose Opioid Quantified with Infrared Pupillometry
studies.design: prospective volunteer dose-escalation study to a respiratory endpoint, repeated-measures ANOVA with Tukey-Kramer post hoc tests
studies.population: healthy volunteers (13 enrolled; 2 withdrew for remifentanil-induced nausea and vomiting, 1 excluded for blink artifacts); 4 women and 6 men, age 29 +/- 3 y, weight 71 +/- 9 kg, haemoglobin 12.9 +/- 1.1 g/dl
studies.condition: remifentanil infusion started at 0.05 mcg/kg/min; after 15 min a 0.1 mcg/kg bolus with the infusion increased by 0.025 mcg/kg/min, then every 5 min a further 0.025 mcg/kg/min increase with each bolus 0.05 mcg/kg larger than the last, until SpO2 <=85% or TcCO2 80 mmHg (typically ~30 min); nasal oxygen 3 L/min throughout
studies.device: NeurOptics (Irvine, CA) portable infrared pupillometer; 800-ms light flash at the start of each 3.2-s scan; reflex amplitude = starting minus minimum diameter; NPi is a proprietary unitless 0-5 index with values above 3 considered normal

measures.units: mm (predrug baseline vs maximal desaturation at SpO2 85%)
measures.p_or_stat: P < 0.0001 (repeated-measures ANOVA); 15 min post-desaturation 4.1 +/- 1.2 mm
measures.evidence_text: Table 1 pupil diameter: predrug baseline 5.6 +/- 0.9 mm, maximal desaturation 2.5 +/- 0.2 mm, 15 min postdesaturation 4.1 +/- 1.2 mm, P < 0.0001. Mean minimum diameter at maximal desaturation 2.5 mm (range 2.2 to 2.8 mm); nonlinear fit minimum 2.3 mm. Adding a light stimulus reduced pupil size by a further 0.3 mm.

measures.units: mm (pupillary light reflex amplitude; predrug baseline vs maximal desaturation)
measures.p_or_stat: P < 0.0001; fractional decrease at desaturation 84 +/- 4% vs an 81 +/- 5% decrease in pupil area (both P < 0.05 vs baseline and 15-min values)
measures.evidence_text: Table 1 pupil light reflex amplitude: baseline 2.5 +/- 0.4 mm, maximal desaturation 0.4 +/- 0.1 mm, 15 min postdesaturation 1.4 +/- 0.6 mm, P < 0.0001. Reciprocal fit of the light reflex at the nadir: mean 0.4 mm, fit parameter 0.3 mm. Reflex amplitude was linearly related to pupil diameter across all measurements (P < 0.0001).

measures.units: NPi (Neurological Pupil index, unitless 0-5)
measures.p_or_stat: P = 0.0049; NPi at desaturation fell by 6.7 +/- 2.5% versus baseline; baseline and desaturation values differ significantly from each other
measures.evidence_text: Table 1 NPi: baseline 4.6 +/- 0.2, maximal desaturation 4.3 +/- 0.2, 15 min postdesaturation 4.4 +/- 0.4, P = 0.0049. Although statistically significant, NPi remained well within the normal range (>3) despite near-maximal opioid effect - a key dissociation between NPi and the raw reflex.

measures.units: mm2 (pupil area)
measures.p_or_stat: P < 0.0001; fractional decrease in pupil area 81 +/- 5%
measures.evidence_text: Table 1 pupil area: baseline 24.9 +/- 8.2 mm2, maximal desaturation 4.9 +/- 0.9 mm2, 15 min postdesaturation 13.9 +/- 7.3 mm2, P < 0.0001.

studies.authors: McKay RE, Larson MD
studies.title: The effect of opioids on the light-off pupillary reflex
studies.journal: Journal of Anesthesia, Analgesia and Critical Care
studies.design: prospective volunteer study with two remifentanil infusion-recovery sequences on the same day separated by at least 30 min washout; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05391555
studies.population: healthy adults, ASA 1-2, age 40-60, BMI < 35 kg/m2; age 49 +/- 6 y, weight 66 +/- 8 kg, 5 female and 5 male. Four did not complete sequence 2 because of nausea; final data 16 light-off trials, 10 paired PUAL/LO comparisons, 6 paired NPi/LO comparisons
studies.condition: remifentanil 0.2 mcg/kg/min for 5 min then 0.3 mcg/kg/min for 5 min; expected effect-site concentrations about 4-6 ng/mL
studies.device: NeurOptics PLR-3000 for pupillary unrest in ambient light (PUAL) and the light-off reflex; NeurOptics NPi-200 for NPi

measures.units: mm (maximum light-off dilation amplitude)
measures.p_or_stat: overall change across measures p = 0.0020; maximum LO dilation at peak effect was < 0.15 mm in 5 trials, 0.15 to < 0.20 mm in 3, and 0.20 to 0.54 mm in 8
measures.evidence_text: Baseline maximum light-off dilation 1.79 +/- 0.47 mm, decreasing by more than 85% at peak remifentanil effect. The light-off reflex declined more than pupil diameter (p = 0.0002 sequence 1; p = 0.0258 sequence 2) and more than NPi (p < 0.0001), but not more than PUAL (p = 0.3516). ROC for distinguishing high-toxic from zero-to-moderate opioid effect: AUROC 0.8925 (95% CI 0.7908-0.9942); < 0.20 mm gave iLR 13.50 (1.92-94.92), > 0.70 mm gave iLR 0.02 (0.00-0.17), and 0.200-0.550 mm was indeterminate at iLR 1.65 (0.94-2.91).

measures.units: s (median time to maximum light-off dilation; baseline vs 10 min, sequence 1)
measures.p_or_stat: p < 0.0001; IQR 7.15-7.99 at baseline vs 1.90-5.62 at 10 min. Sequence 2: 7.70 s (IQR 7.29-7.82) vs 3.58 s (IQR 2.44-7.25), p < 0.0001. Overall baseline median 7.72 s (IQR 7.22-7.99). Regression on remifentanil effect-site concentration: beta = -0.55 +/- 0.08 s per ng/mL, p < .001
measures.evidence_text: Time to maximum dilation fell from a median 7.84 s at baseline to 3.06 s at 10 min in sequence 1 (p < 0.0001) and from 7.70 s to 3.58 s in sequence 2 (p < 0.0001), decreasing by 0.55 +/- 0.08 s for every 1 ng/mL rise in remifentanil effect-site concentration.

measures.units: % decrease from baseline (no absolute means or SDs reported in the main text)
measures.p_or_stat: overall change at peak effect p = 0.0020; magnitude of change differed across parameters p = 0.0001 (sequence 1) and p = 0.0005 (sequence 2)
measures.evidence_text: Pupil diameter decreased by more than 48% at peak effect (abstract). No means or SDs are reported in the main text. Pupil diameter changed substantially less than PUAL (p = 0.0001) and less than the light-off reflex.

measures.units: % decrease in pupillary unrest in ambient light (PUAL)
measures.evidence_text: PUAL decreased by more than 85% at peak effect, a significantly larger change than pupil diameter (p = 0.0001).

measures.units: NPi (unitless 0-5); no numeric values, means or SDs reported in the main text
measures.evidence_text: NPi showed no significant change over time (p = 0.2905), and the light-off reflex declined significantly more than NPi (p < 0.0001). Replicates the Rollins 2014 finding that NPi is relatively insensitive to opioid effect.

studies.authors: McKay RE, Kohn MA, Larson MD
studies.title: Pupillary unrest, opioid intensity, and the impact of environmental stimulation on respiratory depression
studies.journal: Journal of Clinical Monitoring and Computing
studies.design: randomized crossover trial; two identical 35-min remifentanil infusions separated by 30-min washout, under interactive (conversation) versus quiet conditions with alternating sequence; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04301895
studies.population: healthy volunteers aged 18-40
studies.condition: remifentanil 0.2 mcg/kg/min for 5 min then 0.3 mcg/kg/min for 5 min; Minto-model target effect-site concentration 4-6 ng/mL; antiemetic prophylaxis aprepitant 40 mg and ondansetron 4 mg
studies.device: NeurOptics PLR-3000 hand-held infrared pupillometer, left eye, 50 microwatt light source at about 350 lx to initiate oscillation; PUAL computed by post hoc FFT of 10-s videos

measures.units: AU (pupillary unrest in ambient light, PUAL); quiet condition, baseline vs 10 min
measures.p_or_stat: p < 0.001; decline at 10 min 90(9)% and at maximum suppression 96(4)%; baseline PUAL range 0.12-0.54 AU, median 0.27, IQR 0.18-0.33; run 1 vs run 2 pre-infusion difference 0.010 (95% CI -0.026 to 0.045, p = 0.5870)
measures.evidence_text: In the quiet condition mean PUAL fell from 0.264 at baseline to 0.022 at 10 min (p < 0.001), an overall decline of 90(9)% at 10 min and 96(4)% at maximum suppression. Environmental stimulation made little difference: interactive minus quiet mean difference -0.007, p = 0.1240, and suppression by 90% occurred in 18/20 quiet versus 19/20 interactive (HR 1.193, 0.625-2.278, p = 0.593). AUROC for high versus absent-to-moderate opioid exposure was 0.9459 (0.8957-0.9961) quiet and 0.9671 (0.9384-0.9958) interactive (difference p = 0.3588), pooled 0.957 (0.929-0.985). Likelihood ratios: PUAL 0.00-0.04 LR 14.6 (5.59-38.10); PUAL >= 0.13 LR 0.017 (0.004-0.069); between 0.04 and 0.13 indeterminate at LR 1.15 (0.706-1.861).

measures.units: % decline from baseline (absolute means and SDs are in Table 3, which was not reproduced in the available text)
measures.p_or_stat: pupil diameter declined 49.9% +/- 6.4% versus a PUAL decline of 95.1% +/- 4.2% (t test, p < 0.0001)
measures.evidence_text: Pupil diameter declined 49.9% +/- 6.4% while PUAL declined 95.1% +/- 4.2% (p < 0.0001): pupillary unrest is roughly twice as responsive to opioid as static miosis. No separate light reflex measures (constriction velocity or latency) are reported.

measures.units: % decline from baseline at 10 min of remifentanil (mean +/- SD of the percent decline; absolute mm values remain unavailable because Table 3 is not reproduced in the accessible text)
measures.p_or_stat: pupil diameter decline versus PUAL decline, paired t test p < 0.0001
measures.evidence_text: "49.9% +/- 6.4% diameter decline versus 95.1% +/- 4.2% PUAL decline, t test p < 0.0001, Table 3". This upgrades the previously direction-only pupil_diameter_mm record for this study: remifentanil roughly halved pupil diameter, whereas pupillary unrest was almost abolished.
measures.source_location: full text results section (re-available), referring to Table 3

measures.units: % decline in pupillary unrest in ambient light (PUAL) from baseline at 10 min
measures.p_or_stat: p < 0.0001 for the PUAL-versus-diameter decline contrast; average PUAL decline reported as 90(9)% at 10 min and 96(4)% at maximum suppression
measures.evidence_text: "49.9% +/- 6.4% diameter decline versus 95.1% +/- 4.2% PUAL decline, t test p < 0.0001, Table 3"; "90(9)% at 10 min and 96(4)% at maximum suppression (Table 3)"; "Baseline PUAL ranged from 0.12 to 0.54 AU (median 0.27, IQR 0.18 to 0.33)".

studies.authors: McKay RE, Larson MD
studies.title: Detection of opioid effect with pupillometry
studies.design: prospective volunteer study comparing multiple pupillary parameters at baseline and at peak remifentanil effect, with a desaturated versus non-desaturated subgroup comparison
studies.population: volunteers
studies.condition: remifentanil infusion; measurements at baseline and 10 min
studies.device: infrared pupillometer with PUAL derived by fast Fourier transform (model not stated in the available text)

measures.units: AU (pupillary unrest in ambient light, PUAL)
measures.p_or_stat: percent decline at 10 min 93.96 +/- 5.80%; baseline PUAL range 0.12-0.45 AU
measures.evidence_text: Table 1 PUAL: baseline 0.276 +/- 0.102 AU, 10 min 0.016 +/- 0.003 AU, percent decline 93.96 +/- 5.80%. Desaturated vs non-desaturated at 10 min: 0.009 vs 0.022 AU. PUAL showed by far the largest fractional change of any parameter measured.

measures.units: mm
measures.p_or_stat: percent decline at 10 min 49.75 +/- 6.91%
measures.evidence_text: Table 1 pupil diameter: baseline 4.41 +/- 0.56 mm, 10 min 2.19 +/- 0.26 mm, percent decline 49.75 +/- 6.91%. At oxyhaemoglobin desaturation pupil diameter was 1.8-2.6 mm. Desaturated vs non-desaturated at 10 min: 2.15 vs 2.24 mm.

measures.units: mm/s
measures.p_or_stat: percent decline at 10 min 65.24 +/- 15.64%
measures.evidence_text: Table 1 constriction velocity: baseline 3.30 +/- 0.51 mm/s, 10 min 1.12 +/- 0.46 mm/s, percent decline 65.24 +/- 15.64%. At desaturation constriction velocity was 0.4-1.6 mm/s. Desaturated vs non-desaturated at 10 min: 0.88 vs 1.36 mm/s.

measures.units: % reflex (percent constriction)
measures.p_or_stat: percent decline at 10 min 66.39 +/- 15.72%
measures.evidence_text: Table 1 % reflex: baseline 37.35 +/- 4.81, 10 min 12.30 +/- 5.03, percent decline 66.39 +/- 15.72%. At desaturation % reflex was 5-17. Desaturated vs non-desaturated at 10 min: 10.4 vs 14.2.

measures.units: NPi (Neurological Pupil index, unitless 0-5)
measures.p_or_stat: P = 0.7266 (no significant change)
measures.evidence_text: Table 1 NPi: baseline 4.18 +/- 0.30, 10 min 4.24 +/- 0.30, no significant change (P = 0.7266). The authors also note a cited report (Rollins et al.) of only a 6% decrease in NPi with prolonged remifentanil infusion and supplemental oxygen.

measures.units: units not labelled in the available table; the magnitude is consistent with seconds (i.e. ~218 ms vs ~221 ms) but this is NOT stated in the source
measures.p_or_stat: stated as no significant change; no p-value given in the available table
measures.evidence_text: Table 1 latency: baseline 0.218 +/- 0.018, 10 min 0.221 +/- 0.022, reported as showing no significant change. The units are not printed in the available text, so the values are recorded exactly as seen and must be confirmed against the published table before use.

studies.authors: Barvais L, Engelman E, Eba JM, Coussaert E, Cantraine F, Kenny GN
studies.title: Effect site concentrations of remifentanil and pupil response to noxious stimulation
studies.design: prospective stepwise dose-escalation study under propofol target-controlled infusion
studies.population: healthy ASA I/II surgical patients
studies.condition: propofol TCI to loss of consciousness, then remifentanil effect-site concentration raised in 1 ng/mL steps from 0 to 5 ng/mL; pupil response to a 100 Hz tetanic stimulus (T100) measured at loss of consciousness and at each remifentanil plateau

measures.units: mm (pupillary reflex dilatation to a 100 Hz tetanic stimulus; baseline = remifentanil 0 ng/mL, impaired = 5 ng/mL)
measures.p_or_stat: inverse correlation between T100 pupil dilatation and remifentanil effect-site concentration over 0-5 ng/mL, R2 = 0.68
measures.evidence_text: Pupil dilatation to T100 fell progressively from 1.55 (SD 0.72) mm to 0.01 (SD 0.03) mm as remifentanil effect-site concentration rose from 0 to 5 ng/mL (R2 = 0.68). The authors state T100 dilatation was more sensitive to opioid than pupil diameter measured before and after the tetanus. Per-step pupil diameters and p-values were behind the access restriction and are not recorded.

studies.authors: Pickworth WB, Welch P, Henningfield JE, Cone EJ
studies.title: Opiate-induced pupillary effects in humans
studies.journal: Methods and Findings in Experimental and Clinical Pharmacology
studies.volume_pages: 11(12):759-763 (the available record displays January 1990 while other sources cite this volume as 1989; PMID 2626082)
studies.design: human volunteer study of static and dynamic pupillary responses across several opioids
studies.population: human volunteers
studies.condition: morphine, heroin, codeine, oxycodone, oxymorphone and hydrocodone (doses not stated in the available record)
studies.device: Pupilscan handheld pupillometer (described in the source as newly developed)

measures.units: mm (no values available in the available record)
measures.p_or_stat: described as dose-related; no numbers, means or p-values available on the available page
measures.evidence_text: All of the opioids tested reduced pupil size in a dose-related way. Doses, baseline and post-dose diameters, and p-values are not available on the available page.

measures.units: mm/s (no values available in the available record)
measures.evidence_text: The opioids slowed the speed of constriction to a light stimulus. No numeric values are available on the available page.

measures.units: redilation velocity after a light stimulus (no values available)
measures.evidence_text: Redilation velocity after the light stimulus was also reduced. The authors concluded that opioids systematically alter dynamic pupillary responses and that these measures may help quantify drug-induced impairment.

studies.authors: Rottach K, Wohlgemuth WA, Dzaja AE, Eggert T, et al.
studies.title: Effects of intravenous opioids on eye movements in humans: possible mechanisms
studies.design: experimental human study with magnetic search coil eye-movement recording before and after IV opioid
studies.population: four normal subjects
studies.condition: intravenous pethidine and fentanyl; doses are not stated in the available abstract (secondary citations elsewhere on the page mention 0.1 mg IV fentanyl and 100 mg pethidine, but these are secondhand and unconfirmed)
studies.device: magnetic search coil technique

measures.units: presence/absence of downbeat (vertical) nystagmus and saccadic intrusions; no frequency or amplitude values reported
measures.p_or_stat: no p-values reported; effects lasted 10 to 15 minutes
measures.evidence_text: All four subjects showed a transient disturbance of eye fixation with downbeat nystagmus plus saccadic intrusions and oscillations (square wave jerks and saccadic pulses), lasting 10 to 15 minutes. Note this is DOWNBEAT (vertical) nystagmus, not horizontal gaze nystagmus.

measures.units: gain (dimensionless); no values reported
measures.p_or_stat: described only as 'moderately decreased'; no numbers or p-values in the abstract
measures.evidence_text: The gain of sinusoidal vestibulo-ocular reflex and smooth pursuit was moderately decreased, and vertical pursuit showed an upward velocity offset. The authors hypothesised cerebellar dysfunction, possibly through inhibition of parallel fibre activation of Purkinje cells, with opioid binding sites in the vestibular nuclei contributing to vertical vestibular imbalance.

studies.authors: Feit J, Nowińska E, Pasgreta K, Lasń W, Walecki P, Gorzelańczyk EJ
studies.title: Effect of a single dose of methadone on saccadic refixations in opioid addicted subjects with HIV (+) and HIV (-)
studies.volume_pages: conference abstract no. 1903 (volume and pages not stated on the available page)
studies.design: within-subject pre/post single-dose design in two groups (HIV-negative and HIV-positive); conference abstract
studies.population: 60 opioid-addicted patients in a methadone substitution programme: 29 HIV-negative and 31 HIV-positive
studies.condition: a single therapeutic dose of methadone (mg amount not stated); testing before and 1.5 hours after administration
studies.device: saccadometer diagnostic system (Latency Test)

measures.units: ms (no values reported)
measures.p_or_stat: reported as statistically significant in HIV-negative subjects; latency and amplitude changes also described as statistically significant in HIV-positive subjects. No means, SDs or exact p-values are given in the abstract
measures.evidence_text: Latency duration after methadone "increases significantly in HIV(-) subjects". Latency duration and amplitude after methadone are also described as statistically significant in HIV(+) subjects. No numeric values are reported.

measures.units: deg/s (no values reported)

studies.journal: National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (report DOT HS 812 959)

measures.units: odds ratio for 'constricted versus normal' pupil size in darkness, narcotic analgesics versus no-drug cases (pupil size was never recorded in mm)
measures.p_or_stat: B = 3.92, SE = 1.07, Wald = 13.58, significant at the corrected threshold p < .0022; OR = 50.61, 95% CI 6.28-407.93. Constricted vs normal in direct light OR = .01 (95% CI .0002-.64, not significant at the corrected threshold); in room light OR = 13.47 (95% CI .34-539.60, not significant). For CNS depressants, constricted vs normal in darkness OR = 2.17 (95% CI .27-17.34, not significant); pupil size was not a significant predictor for CNS stimulants. Bivariate: pupil size in darkness chi-square = 862.56, Cramer's V = .54; room light chi-square = 516.70, V = .42; direct light chi-square = 316.27, V = .33
measures.evidence_text: Constricted pupils in near-total darkness were the single strongest pupillary discriminator of narcotic analgesic cases from no-drug cases (OR = 50.61, 95% CI 6.28-407.93), and were NOT significant for CNS depressants or stimulants - directly supporting darkness-condition miosis as opioid-specific. No millimetre values are reported anywhere in the report.
measures.source_location: full text Table 16 and bivariate analyses

measures.units: odds ratio for 'droopy versus normal' eyelids, narcotic analgesics versus no-drug cases
measures.p_or_stat: narcotic analgesics B = 2.66, SE = .78, Wald = 11.55, significant at the corrected threshold p < .0022; OR = 14.29, 95% CI 3.08-66.26. CNS depressants B = 1.30, SE = .50, Wald = 6.69, OR = 3.66, 95% CI 1.37-9.78. Bivariate: Cramer's V = .43, chi-square = 269.66
measures.evidence_text: Droopy eyelids (ptosis) were strongly associated with narcotic analgesic cases (OR = 14.29, 95% CI 3.08-66.26) and more weakly with CNS depressants (OR = 3.66, 95% CI 1.37-9.78). Percentages of cases by eyelid status within each drug category are not reported.

measures.units: odds ratio for 'not impaired versus impaired' horizontal gaze nystagmus versus no-drug cases
measures.p_or_stat: narcotic analgesics B = 2.27, SE = 1.02, OR = 9.71, 95% CI 1.31-72.20, NOT significant after correction. CNS depressants B = -2.85, SE = .56, Wald = 26.12, significant; OR = .06, 95% CI .02-.17. CNS stimulants B = 1.21, OR = 3.35, 95% CI .93-12.08, not significant. Bivariate: Cramer's V = .77, chi-square = 835.05. Vertical gaze nystagmus was excluded from the multivariate model for expected-frequency violations; bivariate Cramer's V = .48, chi-square = 329.46
measures.evidence_text: Horizontal gaze nystagmus did not significantly discriminate narcotic analgesic cases after correction (OR = 9.71, 95% CI 1.31-72.20), whereas it was a strong discriminator for CNS depressants (OR = .06 for 'not impaired', i.e. HGN impairment strongly predicted depressants). This is the key dissociation: HGN marks alcohol/depressant impairment, miosis and ptosis mark opioids.
measures.source_location: full text Tables 14-16 and bivariate analyses

measures.units: odds ratio for lack of convergence (versus presence) relative to no-drug cases
measures.p_or_stat: narcotic analgesics B = -.012, OR = .99, 95% CI .22-4.36. CNS depressants B = .18, OR = 1.20, 95% CI .42-3.46. CNS stimulants B = -1.31, SE = .49, OR = .27, 95% CI .10-.70
measures.evidence_text: Lack of convergence carried essentially no information for narcotic analgesic cases (OR = .99, 95% CI .22-4.36) and none for CNS depressants, reaching significance only for CNS stimulants (OR = .27, 95% CI .10-.70).

CAUTION: the paper's own abstract claims antisaccade latency was significantly INCREASED after methadone (p=0.03 HIV-negative, p=0.04 HIV-positive); those p-values in fact match the duration results, so the abstract and results sections contradict each other on the direction of the antisaccade latency change.

measures.evidence_text: "in contrast to the HIV(+) subjects (mean before: 345.8 ms +/-128.2; after: 321.65 ms +/-112.8), where there was no statistically significant difference (p=0.35)."

measures.units: ms, antisaccade duration in HIV-positive methadone patients, before versus after the dose
measures.evidence_text: "An increase of the mean duration values in HIV(-) (mean before: 55.8 ms +/-10.8; after: 60 ms +/-10.8; p=0.03) and HIV(+) (mean before: 60.1 ms +/-11.1; after: 65.3 ms +/-12.1; p=0.04) subjects after the administration of a therapeutic dose of methadone was observed."

measures.evidence_text: "Pupils constricted to 2.1 +/- 0.7 and 4.2 +/- 1.2 mm at the end of the 2-h opioid infusion", "equivalent to miosis of 4.3 +/- 0.7 and 3.0 +/- 1.2 mm, respectively" (hydromorphone, morphine).

measures.evidence_text: "the average z-pupil size before oxycodone intake is -0.212 and after oxycodone intake is -0.985" (bright light, about 500 lux). The z-shift is about half that seen in dim light, consistent with reduced discrimination under bright illumination.

studies.design: randomized, double-blind, triple-dummy, active- and placebo-controlled, single-dose, six-period crossover study at one US clinical research unit (March to December 2016), with at least 5 days of washout between treatments
studies.population: healthy adults aged 18-55, BMI 33.0 kg/m2 or less, who were non-dependent recreational opioid users; 174 enrolled, 75 entered the double-blind phase, 52 completed the pharmacodynamic analysis (45 of 52 male, 86.5%; mean age 28.9 +/- 6.0 y)
studies.condition: all oral: oxycodone DETERx 40 mg intact (fed and fasted), oxycodone DETERx 40 mg chewed (fed and fasted), crushed immediate-release oxycodone 40 mg in solution (fasted, active comparator), and placebo (fed)
studies.device: NeurOptics VIP-200 pupillometer; pupil size assessed at 0.25, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 12 and 24 h post-dose, with Emax computed through 8 h. Lighting conditions are not reported

measures.units: mm of peak pupil effect (Emax through 8 h post-dose); baseline = oral placebo, impaired = crushed immediate-release oral oxycodone 40 mg. IMPORTANT: the article defines Emax only as "the maximum (peak) effect" and never states whether the pupil values are absolute diameters or maximum constriction from baseline; the placebo value of 0.8 mm is far too small for an absolute diameter, so these values are almost certainly maximum constriction (change from baseline) in mm. Absolute baseline diameters are not reported
measures.p_or_stat: placebo was significantly lower than crushed IR oxycodone, p < 0.0001; all four DETERx arms were also significantly lower than crushed IR oxycodone, p < 0.0001. The article reports no pupil p-value for each opioid arm versus placebo, only that there were "statistically significantly greater effects compared with placebo for the majority of secondary endpoints", with pupil diameter in that list
measures.evidence_text: Table 2 (pharmacodynamic population, n = 52), peak effect as mean (SD), columns in order intact DETERx fed, chewed DETERx fed, intact DETERx fasted, chewed DETERx fasted, crushed IR oxycodone fasted, placebo fed: "Pupil diameter, mm 3.1 (0.9) 3.1 (0.8) 2.7 (0.9) 2.9 (0.9) 3.9 (0.8) 0.8 (0.6)". Footnote: "Statistically significantly lower score vs crushed IR oxycodone (p < 0.0001)." "for pupillometry, Emax was calculated through 8 hours postdose".

measures.units: mm of peak pupil effect (Emax through 8 h); baseline = oral placebo, impaired = intact oxycodone DETERx extended-release 40 mg taken fed. Same Emax definitional caveat as above. The other DETERx arms were 3.1 (0.8) chewed fed, 2.7 (0.9) intact fasted and 2.9 (0.9) chewed fasted
measures.p_or_stat: p < 0.0001 versus crushed IR oxycodone 40 mg; no pupil-specific p-value versus placebo is reported
measures.evidence_text: Table 2: "Pupil diameter, mm 3.1 (0.9) 3.1 (0.8) 2.7 (0.9) 2.9 (0.9) 3.9 (0.8) 0.8 (0.6)". The extended-release formulation produced a smaller peak pupil effect than crushed immediate-release oxycodone at the same 40 mg dose, i.e. formulation and route of ingestion modulate the size of the ocular signal at a fixed dose.

studies.authors: Webster L, Cater J, Smith T
studies.title: Effects of buprenorphine buccal film and oral oxycodone on pupil diameter in a respiratory study
studies.design: double-blind, double-dummy, six-treatment, six-period, placebo-controlled, randomized crossover single-centre phase 1 exploratory pharmacodynamics study with 7-day washouts; every participant received both a film and a capsule at each period to maintain blinding (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03996694)
studies.population: 19 enrolled healthy individuals who self-identified as recreational opioid users, confirmed by a day-1 naloxone challenge (18 men, 1 woman, aged 27-41); 15 completed the study and 16 completed at least two treatments (figures report n = 15 and n = 16)
studies.condition: placebo; buprenorphine buccal film 300, 600 and 900 mcg (buccal); immediate-release oxycodone 30 and 60 mg (oral capsule)
studies.device: NeurOptics VIP 200 pupillometer; pupil diameter measured pre-dose and at 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3 and 4 h post-dose

measures.units: mm (numeric means, SDs and changes from baseline are presented only in Figures 4 and 5 and are not given in the text, so no values could be extracted). The extractable quantities are onset times and correlations
measures.p_or_stat: significant constriction versus placebo began at 0.5 h for both oral oxycodone 30 mg and 60 mg, and at 2 h, 1.5 h and 1 h for buprenorphine buccal film 300, 600 and 900 mcg respectively (all p < 0.05)
measures.evidence_text: Onset of significant constriction versus placebo "occurred at 2, 1.5, and 1 hour after dosing with BBF 300, 600, and 900 mcg, respectively"; oxycodone 30 or 60 mg produced significant constriction at 0.5 hours. Constriction with buprenorphine buccal film 300 mcg was significantly less than with oral oxycodone 30 mg at all time points except 4 h and less than 60 mg at all time points; the 600 mcg film was less than both oxycodone doses until 2 h and the 900 mcg film until 1.5 h.
measures.source_location: full text results section (figures not reproduced in the available text)

measures.units: Pearson correlation coefficient between change in mean pupil diameter and change in minute ventilation
measures.p_or_stat: buprenorphine buccal film r = 0.38 to 0.40 (p <= 0.0011); oral oxycodone r = 0.34 to 0.37 (p <= 0.005); placebo r = -0.18 (p = 0.12, not significant)
measures.evidence_text: "Mean minute ventilation and mean pupil diameter were not significantly correlated" under placebo (Pearson r = -0.18; p = 0.12), whereas with active opioid the correlation with change in minute ventilation was r = 0.38-0.40 (buprenorphine buccal film, p <= 0.0011) and r = 0.34-0.37 (oxycodone, p <= 0.005). Relevant to using miosis as a proxy for the degree of central opioid effect.

studies.authors: Slanar O, Nobilis M, Kvetina J, Mikoviny R, Zima T, Idle JR, Perlik F
studies.title: Miotic action of tramadol is determined by CYP2D6 genotype
studies.design: single-dose study in healthy volunteers stratified by CYP2D6 genotype into three groups (homozygous extensive metabolisers, heterozygous extensive metabolisers, poor metabolisers), with repeated pupil measurement over 12 h; no placebo arm (each subject's own pre-dose baseline is the comparator)
studies.population: 21 healthy volunteers, 7 per CYP2D6 genotype group, selected from 270 genotyped medical students
studies.condition: racemic tramadol 100 mg, oral slow-release tablet (Tramal Retard 100); pupil measured at baseline and 2.5, 4, 8 and 12 h post-dose
studies.device: infrared photography with a Sony DSC-F707 digital camera in infrared mode (not a commercial pupillometer), with a 30 mm calibrated standard taped to the cheek below the eye; subjects seated in a dark room after 5 min of dark adaptation, three photographs per eye averaged

measures.units: mm of maximum pupil constriction from each subject's own baseline (Emax, delta mm) after oral tramadol 100 mg in CYP2D6 homozygous extensive metabolisers. The paper reports only changes, not absolute baseline or post-dose diameters. Heterozygous extensive metabolisers 1.25 +/- 0.73 mm; poor metabolisers 0.58 +/- 0.24 mm
measures.p_or_stat: homozygous extensive metabolisers versus poor metabolisers P = 0.0014 (abstract); Table 3 marks the homozygous group significant versus poor metabolisers at p < 0.05. Time to maximum effect 5.71 +/- 2.14 h (homozygous EM), 9.14 +/- 3.02 h (heterozygous EM), 5.64 +/- 3.74 h (PM)
measures.evidence_text: Table 3 (mean +/- SD): Emax (delta mm) homozygous EM "1.83+/-0.95", heterozygous EM "1.25+/-0.73", PM "0.58+/-0.24"; AUD0-12 (mm x h) "12.14+/-6.85", "7.31+/-4.94", "2.64+/-3.20". "The difference in mean pupillary constriction between these two groups was approximately 3-fold" (extensive versus poor metabolisers, from 4 h). All poor metabolisers had Emax below 1 mm while 9 of 14 extensive metabolisers exceeded 1 mm. Spearman correlations: M1 Cmax versus Emax 0.59 (p < 0.01); tramadol Cmax versus Emax -0.39 (p < 0.05).

measures.units: mm x h, area under the pupil-constriction-versus-time curve over 12 h (AUD0-12) in CYP2D6 homozygous extensive metabolisers after oral tramadol 100 mg; heterozygous extensive metabolisers 7.31 +/- 4.94, poor metabolisers 2.64 +/- 3.20
measures.p_or_stat: homozygous extensive metabolisers significantly greater than poor metabolisers, p < 0.05 (Table 3 marker 'a'); single-point metabolic ratio versus effect rs 0.85 to 0.89, p < 0.01
measures.evidence_text: Table 3: AUD0-12 (mm x h) "12.14+/-6.85" homozygous EM, "7.31+/-4.94" heterozygous EM, "2.64+/-3.20" PM. Shows that at a fixed therapeutic oral dose the size of the ocular signal varies about 4-fold with CYP2D6 genotype - a key caveat for any dose-to-miosis inference in driver monitoring.

studies.authors: Rodieux F, Storelli F, Curtin F, Manzano S, Gervaix A, Posfay-Barbe KM, Desmeules J, Daali Y, Samer CF
studies.title: Evaluation of Pupillometry for CYP2D6 Phenotyping in Children Treated with Tramadol
studies.design: single-centre, open-label interventional study (Geneva Children's Hospital, March 2017 to June 2022; NCT03052218); pupillometry before and 150 min after the first tramadol dose, with each child acting as their own control; no placebo arm
studies.population: 41 children analysed of 50 enrolled (9 excluded), with interpretable pupillometry in 37; 26 boys and 15 girls, mean age 11 y (range 3-15; eligibility 1-15 y). Genotype-predicted CYP2D6 phenotypes 63.4% normal, 29.3% intermediate, 4.9% ultrarapid, 2.4% poor metabolisers
studies.condition: first dose of oral tramadol for emergency-department pain management; protocol dose 2 mg/kg to a maximum of 100 mg, mean administered dose 1.66 mg/kg (SD 0.35). CYP2D6 phenotyping with dextromethorphan 0.15 mg/kg
studies.device: handheld infrared NeurOptics NPi-200 pupillometer; protocol target room light 50-500 lux, measured light averaged 205 lux (range 29-760 lux)

measures.units: mm change in resting pupil diameter from pre-dose to 150 min after oral tramadol (mean decrease 0.81 mm, SD 0.90), equivalent to a mean 14.1% decrease (SD 16.7). Absolute pre- and post-dose diameters in mm are not reported
measures.p_or_stat: p = 0.002; a decrease was seen in 83.8% of children. Ambient light was a significant confounder of the degree of miosis (p = 0.003)
measures.evidence_text: "a decrease in pupil diameter in 83.8% of children (p = 0.002)" with "a mean decrease in restPD of 0.81mm (SD 0.90) and 14.1% (SD 16.7)". The association between miosis and mean lux had p = 0.003, so lighting must be controlled when using miosis as an opioid marker.

measures.units: mm change in pupillary light reflex constriction amplitude from pre-dose to 150 min after oral tramadol (mean decrease 0.45 mm, SD 0.56), equivalent to a mean 17.7% decrease (SD 34.5)
measures.p_or_stat: p = 0.011; a decrease was seen in 78.4% of children
measures.evidence_text: A decrease in reflex amplitude "was seen in 78.4% of children (p = 0.011)", with "a mean decrease in RA of 0.45 mm (SD 0.56) and 17.7% (SD 34.5)". The large SD on the percentage indicates substantial between-child variability.

measures.units: association between degree of miosis and CYP2D6 activity (no coefficient reported)
measures.p_or_stat: dextrorphan/dextromethorphan ratio p = 0.308; M1/tramadol ratio and M1 concentration p = 0.243
measures.evidence_text: "We did not find any relation between the degree of miosis between T0 and T150" and CYP2D6 activity measured by the DOR/DEM ratio (p = 0.308). Negative result contrasting with Slanar2007 in adults; constriction velocity, latency and dilation velocity values are not reported, and the regression tables appeared only as image placeholders.

studies.authors: Peeler CE, Gorgy M, Sadlak N, Sathe S, Tamashunas N, Fiorello MG, Cabral H, Paasche-Orlow MK, Weinstein ZM
studies.title: A Pilot Study of Automated Pupillometry in the Treatment of Opioid Use Disorder
studies.volume_pages: volume, issue and pages not established from the accessible sources (published ahead of print; DOI below)
studies.design: prospective cohort pilot study; automated pupillometry measured six times at regular intervals before and after an opioid agonist therapy dose, with each patient serving as their own control. PROVENANCE CAVEAT: the primary article (journals.lww.com) returned a client error and could not be available; the numeric pupil values below were read from the Boston Medical Center institutional summary of the study, with the design and DOI corroborated by a second secondary source (2 Minute Medicine). They have NOT been verified against the primary text
studies.population: 27 inpatients aged 18-50 with opioid use disorder admitted to Boston Medical Center between March and December 2018 who received opioid agonist therapy recommendations from the inpatient Addiction Consult Service; opioid use confirmed by urine toxicology
studies.condition: first inpatient dose of opioid agonist therapy (methadone or buprenorphine); specific drugs per patient and doses are not reported in the accessible sources
studies.device: NeurOptics NPi-200 handheld automated pupillometer; pupil size measured in dark and bright light conditions, with light-reflex latency, percent constriction and constriction/dilation velocity (mm/s) as secondary outcomes

measures.units: mm, mean pupil size in the dark before the first opioid agonist therapy dose versus 15 min after it
measures.p_or_stat: described as a significant decrease; no p-value is reported in the accessible sources
measures.evidence_text: "Prior to the first OAT dose, the mean pupil size in dark and bright light settings was 4.33mm and 2.96mm, respectively." "At 15 minutes after OAT, mean pupil size decreased significantly to 4.01mm in the dark and 2.71 in bright light." The change persisted at later time points. Patients whose withdrawal was well controlled showed a significantly greater pupil-size change at 60 min than patients with high Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale scores (no p-value given).
measures.source_location: secondary institutional summary quoting the primary article (primary full text inaccessible)

measures.units: mm, mean pupil size in bright light before the first opioid agonist therapy dose versus 15 min after it (the summary prints the post-dose figure as "2.71" without a unit, in a sentence whose other values are in mm)
measures.p_or_stat: described as a significant decrease; no p-value reported
measures.evidence_text: "At 15 minutes after OAT, mean pupil size decreased significantly to 4.01mm in the dark and 2.71 in bright light." Note the magnitude of change is small (about 0.25-0.32 mm) in already opioid-tolerant patients, in contrast to the multi-millimetre miosis seen in opioid-naive volunteers.
measures.source_location: secondary institutional summary quoting the primary article

measures.units: mm/s (listed as a secondary outcome; no values are given in the accessible sources)
measures.evidence_text: The study lists constriction and dilation velocity "(mm/s)" and light-reflex latency and percent constriction among its measures, but no velocity or latency values appear in the accessible sources, so no direction can be assigned.

studies.authors: Porath AJ, Beirness DJ
studies.title: Predicting categories of drugs used by suspected drug-impaired drivers using the Drug Evaluation and Classification Program tests
studies.design: retrospective analysis of existing Drug Evaluation and Classification (DEC) case records with multinomial and binary logistic regression against a no-drug referent group; opinions confirmed by blood toxicology
studies.population: 1,512 DEC evaluations of suspected drug-impaired drivers plus 180 no-drug referent cases, from DEC coordinators in 11 US states for evaluations between 22 April 2000 and 24 December 2012. The narcotic analgesic (opioid) subgroup was n = 194; other categories were CNS depressants n = 431, CNS stimulants n = 166, cannabis n = 541
studies.condition: toxicologically confirmed narcotic analgesic (opioid) presence at the time of a roadside/station drug influence evaluation; specific drugs, doses and blood concentrations are not reported by category
studies.device: standard Drug Influence Evaluation procedure (pupil size estimated against a pupillometer card under room light, near-total darkness and direct light; eyelid condition, reaction to light, horizontal gaze nystagmus and convergence assessed by the officer). Pupil size was analysed categorically (constricted/normal/dilated), never in millimetres

measures.units: odds ratio for constricted versus normal pupil size in darkness, narcotic analgesic cases versus no-drug cases (95% CI 6.28 to 407.78). Pupil size was recorded categorically, not in millimetres
measures.p_or_stat: B = 3.92, SE = 1.07, Wald chi-square = 13.58, significant at the Bonferroni-corrected P < .0022
measures.evidence_text: Table 3, narcotic analgesics versus no-drug cases: "Constricted vs. normal pupil size in darkness | 3.92 | 1.07 | 13.58* | 50.60 | 6.28-407.78". This is the single strongest ocular predictor of opioid presence in the model and supplies the quantitative odds ratio that the related NHTSA analysis in the existing evidence base reported only directionally. Pupil size in room light and direct light did not enter the narcotic model, and the overall 22-indicator model classified 89.2% of narcotic analgesic cases correctly.

measures.units: odds ratio for droopy versus normal eyelids, narcotic analgesic cases versus no-drug cases (95% CI 3.10 to 66.66); officer-rated categorical judgement, not a measured eyelid aperture or closure percentage
measures.p_or_stat: B = 2.67, SE = 0.78, Wald chi-square = 11.60, significant at the Bonferroni-corrected P < .0022
measures.evidence_text: Table 3, narcotic analgesics versus no-drug cases: "Droopy vs. normal eyelids | 2.67 | 0.78 | 11.60* | 14.38 | 3.10-66.66". This is the best available quantitative eyelid finding for opioids, although it is a subjective categorical rating rather than an instrumented eyelid measure.

measures.units: odds ratio for slow versus normal pupillary reaction to light, narcotic analgesic cases versus no-drug cases (95% CI 2.78 to 63.09); officer-rated categorical judgement of reaction speed, not an instrumented constriction velocity
measures.p_or_stat: B = 2.58, SE = 0.80, Wald chi-square = 10.47, significant at the Bonferroni-corrected P < .0022
measures.evidence_text: Table 3, narcotic analgesics versus no-drug cases: "Slow vs. normal reaction to light | 2.58 | 0.80 | 10.47* | 13.21 | 2.78-63.09". Qualitatively consistent with the instrumented reductions in constriction velocity and amplitude reported in laboratory pupillometry studies.

measures.units: horizontal gaze nystagmus as a predictor of narcotic analgesic presence (no odds ratio reported because it did not reach significance in this model)
measures.p_or_stat: not reported as a significant predictor for narcotic analgesics
measures.evidence_text: Horizontal gaze nystagmus was not a significant predictor for narcotic analgesics, and lack of convergence was significant only for cannabis (OR 3.57). The four significant indicators in the narcotic model were droopy eyelids, constricted pupils in darkness, slow reaction to light, and being under the care of a doctor or dentist (OR 0.07, i.e. narcotic cases were more likely to be under such care after the authors' direction flip).
measures.source_location: full text Table 3 and results text

studies.authors: Gordon AM, Logan BK
studies.title: Methadone and Impaired Driving
studies.journal: Proceedings of the American Academy of Forensic Sciences Annual Scientific Meeting (Toxicology Section abstract K31)
studies.design: retrospective case series of methadone-positive apprehended drivers from a state toxicology laboratory, with a drug recognition expert evaluated subgroup in which methadone was the only significant finding; conference abstract
studies.population: 629 drivers with methadone-positive blood samples submitted to the Washington State Toxicology Laboratory; a subgroup of 32 had a drug recognition expert evaluation with methadone as the only significant finding
studies.condition: methadone detected in blood in apprehended drivers: mean 0.21 mg/L and median 0.15 mg/L in the full group; mean 0.26 mg/L and median 0.27 mg/L in the 32-driver DRE subgroup. Doses and routes are unknown
studies.device: standard drug influence evaluation (pupil size estimated under room light, near-total darkness and direct light; eyelid condition and reaction to light rated by the officer)

measures.units: % of methadone-positive drivers described as having droopy eyelids (no comparison group; the abstract does not state the denominator explicitly, though it appears to be the 32-driver DRE subgroup)
measures.p_or_stat: descriptive percentage only; no statistical test or control group
measures.evidence_text: "75% were described as having droopy eyelids." A companion slide deck on the same Washington State dataset (Farrell, 'Methadone and Driving', https://breathtest.wsp.wa.gov/docs/webdms/DRE_Forms/InService08/Methadone%20and%20Driving.pdf) reports the same approximately 75% droopy eyelids for the n = 32 methadone-only DRE group alongside pupils "Constricted in all 3 lighting conditions" and reaction to light "Little to none" - but labels these as a DRE matrix prediction, so they may be expected rather than observed values.

measures.units: mm (no group means reported; pupil size is described only categorically for the group)
measures.p_or_stat: descriptive only
measures.evidence_text: "Pupil sizes were consistently constricted in room light, near darkness, and in direct lighting conditions." No group pupil measurements in millimetres are given.

measures.units: mm, pupil diameter in near-total darkness in a single illustrative case (a 35-year-old man with 0.27 mg/L blood methadone); the same case measured 2.5 mm in room light, described as within the normal range, while the 3.0 mm dark measurement was below the normal range. n = 1, so this is a case observation, not a group statistic
measures.p_or_stat: single case; no statistics
measures.evidence_text: "His pupil sizes were 2.5 mm in room light (within normal range); 3.0 mm in darkness (below normal range)." In the same case horizontal gaze nystagmus, vertical gaze nystagmus and lack of convergence were all absent, and watery eyes were noted. Against the drug-free norms in the existing evidence base (Richman2004: 6.41 +/- 1.55 mm in near-total darkness), a 3.0 mm dark pupil is roughly 2.2 SD below the drug-free mean, whereas the room-light value falls inside the normal range - illustrating why darkness is the discriminating condition for opioids.

studies.authors: Hincker A, Reschke M, Ginosar Y, Haroutounian S
studies.title: Investigation of the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of epidural methadone in healthy volunteers
studies.journal: Society for Obstetric Anesthesia and Perinatology (SOAP) Annual Meeting Abstracts
studies.volume_pages: conference abstract (no volume or pages; the available PDF carries no year, filed under the society's 2020 abstract collection)
studies.design: prospective, double-blind, randomized crossover comparison of two epidural opioids; conference abstract. Route is epidural, so this is a clinical-anaesthesia rather than a driving-relevant exposure
studies.population: 13 healthy volunteers who completed both arms
studies.condition: epidural methadone 4 mg versus epidural morphine 4 mg, given as a bolus through a catheter at the L3-L4 interspace; pupil measured at baseline and 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 and 24 h
studies.device: pupilometer (model not stated in the abstract)

measures.units: mm-h, area under the curve of change in pupil diameter versus time over the first 12 h after epidural morphine 4 mg (95% CI -9.2 to -3.2 mm-h). The epidural methadone 4 mg value was -2.9 mm-h (95% CI -4.8 to -0.9)
measures.p_or_stat: methadone versus morphine p = 0.009
measures.evidence_text: "AUC of change in pupil diameter vs time curve was -6.2mm-hr (CI95 -9.2 to -3.2mm-hr) for morphine" and "-2.9mm-hr (CI95 -4.8 to -0.9 mm-hr; p = 0.009) for methadone." Absolute baseline and post-dose diameters are not reported, and the abstract gives no SDs.

studies.authors: Mangas-Sanjuan V, Pastor JM, Rengelshausen J, Bursi R, Troconiz IF
studies.title: Population pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic modelling of the effects of axomadol and its O-demethyl metabolite on pupil diameter and nociception in healthy subjects
studies.design: population pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic modelling (NONMEM 7.2) of pooled data from two multiple-dose clinical trials with placebo and oral active drug; model parameters rather than group means are reported
studies.population: 74 healthy subjects
studies.condition: oral axomadol 66 to 225 mg (an investigational opioid agonist with noradrenaline reuptake inhibition) or placebo, multiple dosing; pupil diameter and cold pressor nociception as pharmacodynamic endpoints
studies.device: pupillometry (device not stated on the accessible page)

measures.units: mm, Emax of the parent drug's effect on pupil diameter (an INCREASE with rising axomadol plasma concentration; relative standard error 17.4%), with C50 90.7 ng/mL (RSE 27%). The O-demethyl metabolite acted in the opposite direction, reducing pupil diameter linearly with a slope of 0.00967 mm per ng/mL of effect-site concentration (RSE 18.7%)
measures.p_or_stat: model parameter estimates with relative standard errors; no group means, SDs or p-values. Each 0.5 mm change in pupil diameter corresponded to a 10% decrease in cold pressor area under the curve
measures.evidence_text: Parent drug: pupil diameter rose with plasma concentration, Emax 0.79 mm (17.4% RSE), C50 90.7 ng/mL (27% RSE). Metabolite: predicted effect-site concentrations reduced pupil diameter linearly, slope 0.00967 mm.mL/ng (18.7% RSE). An additive model linked the net pupil effect linearly to reduced pain, with each 0.5 mm of pupil change corresponding to a 10% decrease in cold pressor AUC. The authors attribute the opposing directions to the compound's dual opioid-agonist and noradrenaline-reuptake-inhibition mechanisms. Important caveat for driver monitoring: a drug with mixed monoaminergic and opioid action can produce mydriasis from the parent compound and miosis from its active metabolite, so net pupil direction is time- and metabolism-dependent.
